To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“The world has moved away from monetary nonautonomy to regimes with more commitment. The choice of regime is related to the country’s financial and economic development, the recent inflation history, and the country’s political system.”
(i) countries with more financial and economic development tend to have more monetary autonomy, and (ii) countries with more monetary autonomy tend to have less discretion.
(1) the world is moving toward regimes with less discretion; (2) this is happening because of a desire to reduce inflation and to increase the predictability of inflation;
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what monetary regimes countries choose and why.
the following question: How do monetary authorities choose their monetary regimes?
the following question: what are the key determinants of the choice of the monetary regime?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
monetary regimes have been converging toward less discretionary regimes.
the choice of a monetary regime is a function of the level of financial development, inflation history, and the level of economic development.
monetary regimes matter, and that the choice of a regime is a key determinant of the inflation process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the world has moved to a more rule-based monetary policy, and this has contributed to the recent global disinflation.
the world is moving toward monetary regimes with more commitment and less discretion.
there is no one size fits all monetary regime.
The main takeaway from our work is that
monetary regime choice is a key determinant of inflation performance and that the choice of a nominal anchor is a key determinant for regime choice.
monetary policy frameworks with more commitment are associated with better macroeconomic outcomes.
the choice of a monetary regime is a choice about the tradeoff between the costs of discretion and the costs of commitment, and the choice of regime depends on the economic and institutional context.
